lesson.menu_title: The Fine Print You Already Signed
lesson.menu_desc: The terms of service nobody reads, and the modals of obligation and permission in legal English -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- The Fine Print You Already Signed

lesson.grammar_point: modals of obligation and permission in legal language

listenings.text: Nobody is going to read forty pages of terms before ordering dinner, and I would never ask you to. But there are three clauses I always read, and you can find them in five minutes with the search function. First, look for the word liable. That clause tells you what the company says it will not pay for. Second, look for dispute or arbitration. That tells you where you will have to go if something goes wrong, and sometimes it is another country. Third, look for share or third parties. That tells you who else receives your data. And remember that finding a clause is not the same as accepting it. If a clause says the company is never responsible for anything, a court may decide that it is void. The contract is important, but it is not the only thing that protects you.

We have updated our terms of service, and we want to explain the most important changes in plain language. Starting next month, if your order arrives more than forty-five minutes late, you may receive a credit for your next order. You are entitled to a full refund only if the order never arrives. We may share some personal data with payment and delivery partners, but we shall not sell your data to advertisers. You may opt out of marketing messages at any time, and you are not required to give us your birthday. Finally, disputes that cannot be solved by our support team shall be resolved by arbitration. If you continue to use the app after thirty days, you consent to these changes. If you do not agree, you may close your account before then.

reading.rtitle: Nobody Reads It, Everybody Signs It
paras: Most people accept dozens of contracts every year without reading a single line. Every time you open a new app and click I agree, you accept its terms of service, and those terms usually describe your rights and obligations more precisely than any conversation with the company ever will. The fine print is not decoration. It is the contract.

Terms of service are written in a particular kind of English. Obligations are marked with shall and must: the user shall keep the password secret; the company must protect personal data. Permissions are marked with may: the company may change the price, and you may cancel at any time. Prohibitions use may not or shall not, and the difference between may and must is often the difference between an option and a duty.

Two kinds of clauses deserve more attention than the rest. The first limits the company’s liability, for example by saying that it is not responsible for delays or errors. The second decides where a dispute will be resolved: in a court, or in private arbitration, sometimes in another country. Some terms also ask users to waive rights they did not know they had, such as the right to join other consumers in a collective case.

However, a contract is not stronger than the law. In many countries, including Brazil, consumer law protects users from abusive clauses, and a clause that removes all of a company’s liability for its own failures can be void. Personal data also cannot simply be shared with a third party without a legal basis, and in many cases that basis is the user’s consent. So the next time an app says you are not entitled to a refund, the honest answer is: that depends on what the law says, not only on what you clicked.
